header: Attendees: Jamie Park (Redwood AE); Sofia Martinez (Redwood SE); Alex Chen (CTO, Eden); Priya Nair (Lead ML Eng, Eden); Marcus Li (Infra, Eden)
summary: SE-led deep dive on p95/p99 tail latency tradeoffs. Covered streaming vs non-streaming, KV cache behavior, batching, quantization impacts, and network/VPC hop contributions. Agreed next steps include running dedicated benchmarks and sharing security docs.
topics: observability and tracing for tail events
transcript: [00:00] Jamie Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we have about an hour, we'll do a quick agenda then dive into p95/p99 stuff. Sofia will lead the deep dive.
[00:10] Alex Chen: Hi, yeah thanks. we want to understand tail latency — our app needs <100ms p95 for short prompts and p99 is the blocker right now.

[00:18] Sofia Martinez: Great, quick intro: I'm Sofia, infra and latency work at Redwood. We'll cover where tail comes from: model decode, batching, KV cache misses, and network hops — including intra-region egress and VPC NATs.
[00:30] Priya Nair: To be clear, our typical prompt lengths are 40-80 tokens, sometimes we stream incremental completions to the client. we see big spikes when traffic is bursty.
[00:44] Marcus Li: And we run in a VPC with an NGW and a private subnet; occasionally we see 10-20ms additional hops through the NAT. want to know how much Redwood side adds.
[01:05] Sofia Martinez: Good, that context helps. quick question: are you using any caching client-side or at the app layer today?
[01:11] Alex Chen: Minimal, we rely mostly on Redwood to handle caching — hoping prefix caching helps when similar prompts repeat.

[01:20] Sofia Martinez: Ok. One high-level note: p95 is often governed by median-ish factors like model token throughput and batching, p99 tends to expose rare events: cache misses, re-tries, GC pauses, network spikes, cold KV cache misses across hosts.
[01:36] Jamie Park: We'll share the benchmark spreadsheets after this — includes token distribution, seq length histograms, and sample prompts you mentioned.
[01:45] Priya Nair: Cool. Sofia, can you explain KV cache behavior and when misses occur? we've heard 'KV cache warms' but want concrete timings.

[01:53] Sofia Martinez: Sure. Redwood uses per-worker KV caches holding recent key/value kv rows for autoregressive decoding. When a request hits the same model variant and the same cached prefix on the same worker, we serve without reloading weights nor rebuilding KV; that's sub-5ms extra. Misses cause either fetching from remote cache shard or re-creating the KV which is 20-80ms depending on seq len and backend IO.
[02:20] Priya Nair: 20-80ms is significant for p99. what causes fetches from remote shard vs local hit?

[02:27] Sofia Martinez: Rotation and routing: requests are routed to workers by routing policy; if your workload is spread randomly across workers, cold starts will be more. We recommend sticky routing for low-latency customers or elastic hot-shard pinning during pilots.
[02:40] Marcus Li: Sticky routing means stateful affinity? does that conflict with autoscaling?
[02:45] Sofia Martinez: It can if you over-pin. We do hybrid: short-lived sticky windows (30s-2m) plus capacity-aware routing. That keeps cache hit rate high while allowing autoscale to rebalance.
[02:58] Alex Chen: For streaming vs non-streaming: we currently stream partial tokens. does streaming add overhead that increases p99?

[03:06] Sofia Martinez: Two main things: streaming reduces perceived latency for the user but can add small per-frame network overheads. More importantly, it changes batching behavior — streaming requests often flush earlier which prevents large batch aggregation, increasing per-token latency but lowering tail for individual first tokens. For p99 it depends: if you have low QPS, streaming can help by not waiting to build batches; at high QPS, batching is more efficient and reduces both cost and tail if configured properly.
[03:36] Priya Nair: So there's a tradeoff. do you have numbers?

[03:39] Sofia Martinez: We referenced internal benchmarks: at 50 RPS with 40-token prompts, non-streaming with 64 sized batches gave p95 ~45ms p99 ~120ms; streaming (flush-on-first-token) p95 ~30ms p99 ~180ms in that config because of more small batches and occasional KV misses. We'll send the raw sheets.
[04:02] Alex Chen: The p99 widening on streaming is surprising — is that due to network framing?

[04:07] Sofia Martinez: Partially. Also tail comes from workers that missed KV and had to build caches, or a worker experiencing OS-level jitter. We instrument per-worker p99. We recommend investigating the tail sources by correlating request ids with worker ids — Redwood traces can include that if you enable advanced tracing.
[04:27] Marcus Li: On-network: our topology has two extra hops: private NAT, then a transit GW to internet egress. how much should we budget?

[04:34] Sofia Martinez: Typical NAT+transit adds 5-25ms depending on cloud and whether you cross AZs. Cross-AZ egress is common cause of 10-40ms jumps. For tight p99 budget you want same-AZ routing and VPC endpoints where possible. For Redwood Private deployments we can run in your VPC to avoid public egress entirely.
[04:56] Alex Chen: About quantization: we considered int8 quant. does quantization increase or decrease tail?

[05:02] Sofia Martinez: Quantization reduces per-token latency because kernels are faster and memory bandwidth smaller. But p99 can be impacted if quant kernels have cold cache jitters or if you hit fallback paths to float kernels for certain ops. In our experience 4-bit/8-bit quant reduces average and median latency but you must validate p99 on your workload — we'll provide quantization profiles per model.
[05:28] Priya Nair: What about batching policies? we saw that fixed batch sizes reduce latency variance but hurt single-request latency.

[05:35] Sofia Martinez: Right. We support adaptive batching: a queueing window + target max batch size. You can tune the window (5-30ms) to trade off user latency vs throughput. For p99 you often increase the window slightly to smooth bursts; for p95 you may lower it. Also prefix caching reduces effective batch sizes because repeated prefixes don't need full compute.
[05:58] Jamie Park: Quick interruption — Alex, you mentioned target SLOs earlier. can you restate them so we keep focus?
[06:05] Alex Chen: Sure — p95 < 100ms for 40-80 token prompts, p99 < 200ms ideally. If we can't meet p99 we'll accept fallbacks with degraded model for p99 cases but need deterministic behavior.

[06:18] Sofia Martinez: Good, that helps. For deterministic fallbacks we support model variants routing: if a high-cost worker is busy we can route to a slightly smaller quantized variant with deterministic latency cap. That's what we call variant fallback.
[06:31] Priya Nair: How do you measure and attribute tail events? we need logs to debug when p99 spikes occur.

[06:37] Sofia Martinez: We emit request-level traces with timestamps for each stage: ingress, routing decision, KV lookup, model decode start, model decode end, response send. Each trace tags worker id, model variant, quant profile, and batch size. We'll share an example tracing dashboard and a small gRPC trace sample.
[06:55] Marcus Li: Is the tracing data available if we run Redwood Private on-prem?

[06:59] Sofia Martinez: Yes, Private has local telemetry collection; logs can feed to your datadog/elk and we can integrate with your SSO to restrict access. For some regulated customers we ship an agent that writes traces to your KMS-encrypted buckets.
[07:15] Alex Chen: On security: will using Private mean we avoid public internet egress?

[07:20] Jamie Park: Yes, Private runs in your VPC/on-prem. You control KMS, networking, and we can disable outbound egress except for necessary control plane calls. We'll include our SOC2 docs and required architecture diagrams.
[07:32] Priya Nair: Back to tail: you mentioned GC pauses — are those in the Python stack or underlying runtime?

[07:37] Sofia Martinez: Mostly runtime-level; our serving runtimes are C++/Rust-based, but we do have occasional GC-like pauses for memory compaction in certain kernels or the allocator; those are rare but can show at p99. We mitigate with pre-warm pools and memory retention strategies.
[07:55] Alex Chen: Could autoscaling cause p99 spikes during scale events?

[07:59] Sofia Martinez: Yes. Scale-out events cause cold caches on new workers, which can increase p99 for a short window. We manage this with warm pools and staggered scale. For strict p99 customers we recommend Dedicated with reserved capacity to minimize scale churn.
[08:16] Priya Nair: For our pilot, we'd prefer Dedicated — can you describe expected throughput and headroom for our model size?

[08:22] Sofia Martinez: If you share model variant and peak QPS we can size GPU pools. For example, a 70B quantized model on an A100-like machine with our kernels can do ~12-20 tokens/ms depending on batch size; your user-visible latency per request depends on seq len and batching. We'll run an initial bench on Dedicated pilot to validate.
[08:43] Alex Chen: We'll send model info after this call.

[08:47] Sofia Martinez: Great. Next, a quick walkthrough of a p99 postmortem pattern we see: 1) network cross-AZ egress; 2) KV cache miss + remote fetch; 3) worker noise (co-located process); 4) rare kernel fallback; 5) retries from client side doubling requests. If you correlate traces you can usually find the dominant contributor.
[09:09] Marcus Li: Client retries are ours — we have exponential backoff but some clients retry at 200ms which could amplify tail.
[09:16] Jamie Park: Good candidate for optimization: reduce retry aggressiveness, implement jitter, maybe client-side hedging only for critical requests.
[09:24] Priya Nair: About hedging — does Redwood support server-side hedging?

[09:28] Sofia Martinez: We support hedging via routing to multiple model variants in parallel with cancel-on-first-complete; that helps p99 but doubles cost. Use it selectively for high-value requests.
[09:38] Alex Chen: Let's talk observability: what dashboards should we watch during the pilot?

[09:42] Sofia Martinez: Per-route p50/p95/p99, per-worker p99 heatmap, KV cache hit rate, batch-size distribution, and network egress latencies. We'll set up an initial dashboard in the Console and give you editor access.
[09:58] Priya Nair: When you say per-worker p99 heatmap, can we map to host metrics (CPU, PCIe bandwidth)?
[10:03] Sofia Martinez: Yes we correlate host-level telemetry and model-level traces. Often p99 correlates with PCIe saturation or unexpected host interrupts.
[10:13] Alex Chen: For the benchmark run, what sample workload should we provide?

[10:17] Sofia Martinez: Provide: (1) representative prompt set with token lengths, (2) QPS patterns (steady, bursty), (3) streaming vs non-streaming flags, (4) desired SLOs and priority routes. We'll run both streaming and non-streaming benches and return p50/p95/p99 plus trace samples.
[10:32] Marcus Li: For VPC networking we'd like to know recommended CNI configs to avoid extra hops.
[10:36] Sofia Martinez: Use regional endpoints and same-AZ subnets; avoid NAT if possible by using VPC endpoints and private link to the Redwood service. We'll include a recommended VPC diagram.
[10:48] Jamie Park: Alex, any questions on pricing implications? streaming vs non-streaming affects billable token patterns and the cost per request.
[10:55] Alex Chen: We mostly care about unit economics; if hedging doubles cost we might limit it. Also quantization may change perf and cost — we need guidance.

[11:03] Sofia Martinez: We'll include a cost sensitivity table: per-token CPU/GPU cost for float vs int8 vs 4-bit quant and expected throughput numbers. Also show cost impact of hedging and Dedicated reserved pricing.
[11:14] Priya Nair: Will Redwood run the quantization ourselves or do we need to supply quantized checkpoints?

[11:19] Sofia Martinez: We can do model onboarding and recommended quant profiles; for some customers we accept their quantized artifacts if they meet a spec. For strict determinism you may prefer our managed quant to ensure kernel compatibility.
[11:31] Alex Chen: For pilot timeline what's realistic?
[11:34] Jamie Park: If you can provide prompt set and model details by 2026-09-17, Sofia's team can run bench week of 2026-09-21 and we can review results that week.
[11:44] Alex Chen: Sounds good. One more thing: we saw occasional 'worker not ready' errors in logs — how does that map to tail?

[11:50] Sofia Martinez: 'Worker not ready' usually occurs during warm-up or when the worker is evicted for updates. In an autoscale scenario it can spike p99 briefly. Our dedicated pilot avoids that by reserving workers and controlling updates.
[11:59] Priya Nair: Any quick tips we can apply immediately to reduce p99?

[12:03] Sofia Martinez: Yes: 1) enable sticky routing or short affinity windows; 2) use same-AZ endpoints; 3) reduce client retry aggressiveness; 4) consider slight batching window increase to smooth bursts; 5) enable KV pre-warming for known prefixes.
[12:18] Marcus Li: For KV pre-warming — how do we surface prefixes to Redwood?
[12:22] Sofia Martinez: You can upload a small prefix dataset during onboarding or call a pre-warm API with example requests; we'll warm the KV caches across workers.
[12:30] Alex Chen: Okay. Let's talk a little about test telemetry we expect to get back after the bench - will it include sample traces for p99 events?
[12:37] Sofia Martinez: Yes; we'll include a set of trace files and a summary CSV mapping request id -> stage latencies -> worker id -> batch size -> kv_hit boolean.
[12:47] Priya Nair: That CSV should help us correlate with our app logs.
[12:50] Sofia Martinez: Exactly. Also we'll add recommended mitigations itemized per root cause.
[12:57] Jamie Park: Quick recap then next steps — Sofia, can you summarize the main mitigations we recommended?

[13:02] Sofia Martinez: Sure: 1) sticky routing / affinity, 2) pre-warm KV caches, 3) same-AZ routing and VPC endpoints, 4) adaptive batching tuning, 5) quantization validation with p99 checks, 6) consider Dedicated for reserved capacity, 7) selective hedging for critical requests.
[13:20] Alex Chen: We'll send prompts + model info by EOD 2026-09-17. Marcus will share network diagram. We'll expect the bench week of 9/21.
[13:29] Jamie Park: Great. I'll send SOC2 docs and pricing by tomorrow and create the follow-up invite. Any final questions?
[13:36] Priya Nair: One small question: is KV cache global across workers or sharded?
[13:40] Sofia Martinez: Sharded per worker; we do cross-shard fetches for misses which is the expensive path. hence the affinity advice.
[13:48] Alex Chen: Thanks all, this was helpful.
[13:50] Jamie Park: Thanks everyone. end call.
[13:52] (meeting ended)
